name: Railway
description: Railway is an infrastructure platform that deploys any language or framework — Node.js, Python, Go, Ruby — along with databases like PostgreSQL and Redis, with zero Dockerfile configuration required. Nixpacks auto-detects your stack and handles the rest.

useCases.task: Deploy a Node.js, Python, or Go backend server
Host a PostgreSQL or Redis database with automatic backups
Deploy a full-stack app with web server and database together
Run scheduled cron jobs or background workers

setupSteps: Sign up at railway.app (GitHub login recommended)
Create a new project from the dashboard
Connect your GitHub repository or use `railway init` from the CLI
Railway auto-detects your stack with Nixpacks and deploys on every push
Generate an API token at railway.app/account/tokens and set RAILWAY_TOKEN

rateLimits.limit: No hard request rate limits — limits are on compute resources (vCPU, RAM). Deployments are limited to 512MB RAM and 2 vCPU on Hobby plan.
rateLimits.notes: Railway bills purely on resource consumption (CPU + RAM per minute). There are no request-count limits. Hobby plan services sleep after inactivity by default, which reduces costs but introduces cold-start latency.
rateLimits.retryStrategy: Handle application-level retries. Railway provides health checks and automatic restarts on crash.

codeExamples.title: Deploy via railway.json config
codeExamples.notes: Railway injects a PORT environment variable automatically — always use process.env.PORT rather than hardcoding a port. The railway.json schema supports custom build commands, health checks, and restart policies. Run `railway up` to deploy from your terminal without pushing to git.

codeExamples.title: Query Railway API with SDK
codeExamples.notes: The Railway SDK wraps the GraphQL API. Alternatively you can query the Railway GraphQL API directly at https://backboard.railway.app/graphql/v2 with a Bearer token. The SDK is in early development — the GraphQL API is more stable for production automation.

gotchas: Railway removed its free tier in 2023. The Hobby plan has a $5/month minimum charge that applies even if your usage is zero — you will be billed $5 regardless of whether you deploy anything. There is no purely free option; plan accordingly before using Railway for side projects or experiments.

Hobby plan services sleep after a period of inactivity to reduce costs. The first HTTP request after a sleep period incurs a cold-start delay while the container restarts. For production services that require consistent low-latency responses, upgrade to the Pro plan or implement a keep-alive ping (e.g., an uptime monitor hitting /health every 5 minutes).

Railway does not provide a static outbound IP address on the Hobby plan. If any external service you call (a managed database, a payment provider, or a third-party API) requires IP allowlisting for security, you cannot use Railway's Hobby plan — you must upgrade to Pro to get a dedicated static IP.

Persistent volumes in Railway attach to a single service instance only. If you scale a service to multiple replicas, each replica gets its own isolated volume — there is no shared filesystem between replicas. Sharing state across replicas requires an external store (Redis, PostgreSQL, S3) rather than the local filesystem.

reliability.uptimeGuarantee: Uptime SLA not published; ~99.9% in practice
reliability.notes: Railway runs on AWS infrastructure with automatic health checks and container restarts on failure. No published SLA for the Hobby plan. Pro plan customers have access to priority support.

qualityJustification: Excellent developer experience for deploying any app without Dockerfile knowledge (uses Nixpacks for auto-detection). Best Heroku alternative with auto-provisioned databases. Loses points for removing free tier and limited documentation for advanced configurations.
bestFor: Deploying full-stack applications with databases, background workers, and cron jobs — the closest modern replacement for Heroku
